blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: Poilievre Caucus Regroups Amid Trump Tensions and BC Vote
blocks.script:
Good day. Here's your look at Canadian politics for September 24th, 2026.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre's caucus gathered on Parliament Hill this week for the first time this fall sitting, according to POLITICO's Canada Playbook. Officially, the party says it's united. But behind the scenes, sources describe MPs eager to regain political momentum after a summer of internal tension that Poilievre largely left unaddressed.

Playbook reports that Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner hosted a dinner earlier this week in Ottawa drawing about 25 people, including fellow Conservative MPs. One attendee, granted anonymity, described it as an open forum for political discussion on topics like immigration and criminal justice, not a challenge to Poilievre's leadership. No resolutions came out of the gathering.

Divisions within the party also surfaced over how to handle Donald Trump. After the U.S. president criticized Canadian potash, some Conservative MPs, including House Leader Andrew Scheer, pointed to the federal industrial carbon tax as the cause. Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney pushed back hard on social media, accusing his own party of lacking what he called the moral clarity shown by Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe in standing up to Trump. Kenney said it was, in his words, embarrassing that Conservatives seemed more focused on courting Trump-friendly voters than confronting threats to Canadian sovereignty.

Trump himself kept up the pressure this week. CBC reports the president claimed Canada is destroying itself through immigration policy, alleging the country has let in migrants without proper security checks. Federal ministers dismissed the claims as inaccurate.

Meanwhile in the House, Poilievre dismissed the government's new economic bill, C-39, as all talk and no action, according to the Globe and Mail, though he declined to say how his MPs would actually vote on the legislation meant to fast-track major projects.

On the labour front, CBC reports the Carney government is proposing changes to the Canada Labour Code that it says will protect the right to strike, though experts warn legal battles over a controversial section are far from over. Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says a new mediator role bringing public reporting to stalled negotiations will bring what she called sunlight to the bargaining table.

Prime Minister Mark Carney spent part of the week in New York for United Nations General Assembly events, including remarks at an oceans conservation pledging event, before returning to Ottawa. In a New York Times interview flagged by the Globe and Mail, Carney said he has prepared for the remote possibility that Trump could order military action against Canada, calling it unlikely but something his government has considered.

Defence Minister David McGuinty gave a speech in Ottawa this week on Canada's global security alliances, name-checking Japan, Norway, Britain and other partners. Notably, Playbook points out he made zero references to the United States.

In British Columbia, Premier David Eby has called a snap election for October 24th, two years ahead of schedule. The Globe and Mail reports Eby says he needs a strong mandate to deal with economic chaos caused by the Trump administration's trade war. He called the vote even though the opposition BC Conservatives currently have no permanent leader, and despite municipal leaders asking him to avoid overlapping with municipal elections set for a week earlier.

In Ontario, the fallout continues from Sunday's shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville. The Globe and Mail reports the suspect died Monday night, with a postmortem scheduled this week. In the House of Commons, local Liberal MP Chris Malette paid tribute to his constituents, saying his thoughts remain with the Jewish community as residents search for answers.

Also making headlines, Ottawa's city council has voted to rename Trump Avenue after residents said they no longer wanted the street associated with the U.S. president, according to the Globe and Mail's politics newsletter.
talkingPoints: Conservative caucus faces internal strain over how firmly to confront Trump on trade threats, with Jason Kenney publicly breaking ranks.
Trump's rhetoric on Canadian immigration and trade continues to shape domestic political debate ahead of the fall sitting.
BC's snap election adds a provincial flashpoint tied directly to the ongoing Canada-US trade conflict.
Carney government pushes ahead on major projects legislation and labour code reform while managing diplomacy in New York.
Defence policy signals a deliberate distancing from Washington, alongside preparations for even remote worst-case scenarios.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Ottawa's Bill C-39 Meets Manitoba Energy and Charity Rules
blocks.script:
The biggest climate policy story touching your clients this week is Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act. Canada's National Observer reports the bill is facing pushback from political, environmental, and labour groups because it amends several laws to fast-track projects the government deems to be in the national interest. An opinion piece in the same outlet frames the fight as bigger than any one pipeline or transmission line: it's really a fight over what counts as the national interest at all, touching regulatory rules, labour law, environmental assessment, and Indigenous consultation together. For you, the practical read is that this bill is the federal government's main lever for speeding up permitting on energy and infrastructure projects, so watch it if you have clients with exposure to resource or construction timelines.

Alberta is a live case study in that same tension. National Observer reports that scientists, conservationists, and legal experts say the province's caribou land use plans, first ordered by Ottawa back in 2012, still lack the modelling and recovery goals needed to actually protect woodland caribou, because oil and gas development has consistently been prioritized ahead of habitat protection.

British Columbia shows you what physical climate risk looks like once it's no longer theoretical. National Observer's wildfire coverage out of Faulder, near Summerland, follows residents sifting through the ashes of homes destroyed last month. That same wildfire season is now compounding into a business story: the outlet reports Okanagan wineries, Canada's second largest wine region, are dealing with fire damage layered on top of a trade war and provincial trade barriers that are pushing producers toward the brink.

Closer to home, Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list this week. The Crown corporation's 2025 Integrated Resource Plan, filed with the Public Utilities Board, commits to procuring up to 600 megawatts of Indigenous majority owned wind power, building roughly 750 megawatts of new natural gas combustion turbines, and working with Efficiency Manitoba on conservation programs to free up supply. CBC reports Manitoba's Climate Action Team argues the plan under-invests in battery storage, contrasting Manitoba's roughly five megawatts planned over ten years with Ontario's build-out of thousands of megawatts by 2028. That's a live debate for any client with utility or infrastructure exposure in this province.

On the nonprofit side, there's a real governance shift underway at the Canada Revenue Agency that boards need to know about. Since the start of 2026, the CRA's Charities Directorate has stopped offering pre-approval or advance review of changes to a charity's stated purposes, according to Miller Thomson's charity law practice. That means a board that changes its mission at an annual meeting now has to file the change and find out later whether the CRA agrees, with the charity's registered status on the line if it doesn't. Philanthropic Foundations Canada notes the CRA issued new guidance in May with model purposes to help with drafting, but the underlying risk shift to charities themselves stands. Separately, the CRA retired its fax line entirely as of April 1st, pushing all charity filings, including the annual T3010 return, onto its online portal, and it has stepped up enforcement of the 5% disbursement quota using that same T3010 data. If you have clients naming a private foundation or charity in an estate plan, or sitting on a board themselves, this is the year to confirm their governance paperwork and their advisors are actually keeping pace with these changes.
talkingPoints: Bill C-39 is Ottawa's main tool for fast-tracking energy and infrastructure permits, worth tracking for project timelines.
Alberta's caribou land use plans still favor oil and gas development over habitat recovery goals, say experts.
Okanagan wineries face wildfire damage plus a trade war, a double hit worth knowing for BC-exposed clients.
Manitoba Hydro's new resource plan leans on gas turbines and wind, with critics flagging thin battery storage investment.
CRA no longer pre-approves charity purpose changes, so any client's foundation should get its governance reviewed this year.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Meta Goes All In On Muse At Connect
blocks.script:
Meta held its annual Connect event in Menlo Park this week, and CEO Mark Zuckerberg used his keynote to signal that the company is betting heavily on its AI agent, Muse. According to TechCrunch, Muse is being pushed across Meta's hardware lineup, including a new small wearable device likened to a Tamagotchi that gives the assistant its own physical home, and new camera-free AI glasses designed to be lighter with up to twelve hours of battery life.

Tech analyst Ben Thompson, writing in his Stratechery newsletter, has been tracking what this expansion means for the wider e-commerce battle between Meta, Amazon and Walmart. Thompson argues that Meta's real challenge is getting Muse users to shop through the platform without hitting a wall of Amazon products it cannot easily show ads against. One option he raises is Meta building on its existing 2023 advertising partnership with Amazon to let Muse surface Amazon ads directly.

But Thompson thinks the more interesting path runs through Walmart. He points out that Walmart moved quickly to join OpenAI's Instant Checkout program earlier this year, only to pull back after seeing conversion rates roughly a third of what it gets on its own site, along with smaller basket sizes. Even so, Thompson says that willingness to jump in fast suggests Walmart could be an early partner for Muse as well, especially since Meta's approach would let Muse send shoppers to Walmart to complete purchases rather than charging a fee per transaction the way OpenAI's checkout system does.

Thompson's argument is that if Walmart signs on, Meta could play a long game against Amazon, chipping away purchases one shopper at a time. He notes that Amazon's advantage rests on massive physical logistics infrastructure, but that infrastructure only stays efficient if it is fully utilized. Every purchase that goes elsewhere raises the relative cost of everything else moving through Amazon's warehouses and delivery network.

Separately, Stratechery published an interview with Colossus editor-in-chief Jeremy Stern, who recently wrote a widely discussed profile of Zuckerberg. Stern, a former U.S. Army explosive ordnance disposal officer turned writer, discussed his path into profile writing and his approach to getting tech leaders to open up, following earlier profiles of figures including Palmer Luckey and Anduril and Palantir executives.

Beyond Meta, TechCrunch reported a wave of other AI product updates this week. OpenAI's ChatGPT mobile app is adding voice based agentic features for Pro and Plus subscribers through its Work tab. YouTube rolled out several AI tools, including a conversational Ask Music feature, custom Gemini powered feeds that let users describe the videos they want to see, and new AI tools for creators inside YouTube Studio. Spotify is bringing its Taste Profile feature to US Premium users, letting listeners see how the algorithm reads their preferences and adjust it using natural language.

On the research side, TechCrunch reported that Anthropic says its biology lab has already produced a significant discovery, though the company is keeping humans in the loop rather than letting its Claude model operate independently in the lab for now.

On policy, the BBC reported that the United States has rejected calls from OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face's Clement Delangue for coordinated global AI risk standards. The BBC also reported that OpenAI is providing Ukraine with access to its GPT model for cyber defense purposes, and that the company's systems were involved in a data breach affecting Australia's Medicare system. Separately, the FBI is investigating a hacker claim of stolen staff data, unrelated to OpenAI.
talkingPoints: One, Meta is pushing Muse into hardware, wearables and glasses, showing it sees the AI agent as central to its future rather than a side feature.
Two, Walmart's early but rocky experience with OpenAI's Instant Checkout may still make it a likely partner for Meta's Muse, according to Stratechery's analysis.
Three, the long term contest over agentic shopping could quietly reshape competition between Amazon, Walmart and Meta.
Four, major platforms including YouTube, Spotify and ChatGPT are racing to add conversational and agentic AI features for everyday users.
Five, the US government's rejection of global AI safety standards puts it at odds with leading AI labs pushing for coordinated oversight.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Law Sentencing, Cancer Gift, and Tendon Science
blocks.script:
Sentencing hearings began this week in Newmarket, Ontario, for Kenneth Law, a former chef who pleaded guilty in May to aiding fourteen suicides, admitting he ran websites that sold lethal chemicals to vulnerable people worldwide, CBC reports. Court documents show he shipped sodium nitrite to more than forty countries, with seventy nine linked deaths in the United Kingdom alone, CTV reports. Families gave victim impact statements this week, some for victims as young as fourteen.

On a better note, the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation in Toronto received an anonymous gift of one hundred million dollars this week, the largest single donation in the foundation's history, CBC reports. It goes to the cancer centre's top priorities in research, education and care, a useful data point if clients are weighing major gifts to Canadian hospital foundations.

In the mountains, Outside reports the climbing season on Manaslu, Nepal's second most popular eight thousand metre peak, ended early after heavy snow and a deadly avalanche. Four climbers died this season. Anyone booking a high altitude expedition should treat that as current risk, not just headline risk.

Also from Outside, a writer spent three days at Idaho's North Fork Championship watching elite kayakers handle extreme whitewater. Her takeaway: repeated, controlled exposure to real danger builds focus and calm that avoidance never will, which is as good an argument for progressive training as any.

And if a client loves to climb, Outside published a list of six climbing towns that are still affordable, worth a look for anyone weighing a relocation or a second property built around an outdoor training lifestyle.

Last one, for anyone lifting seriously. Stronger By Science highlights new work from German researcher Falk Mersmann on tendon injuries. His research shows tendons adapt within a strain window of roughly four and a half to six and a half percent of resting length, regardless of whether you train heavy or light, fast or slow. Published data out of Humboldt University in Berlin found that during squats at forty percent of one rep max, strain on the patellar tendon ranged from two point six percent in some lifters to nearly six percent in others. Same load, very different stimulus. It's a case for individualized rehab and loading rather than one size fits all programs, and researchers say personalized testing protocols are still being developed.
talkingPoints: Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation just landed a hundred million dollar anonymous gift, the largest in its history.
Sentencing began for Kenneth Law in Ontario, a stark reminder of how online sales of lethal chemicals evaded regulators for years.
Manaslu's climbing season ended early after a deadly avalanche killed four, worth flagging for any client planning a Himalayan trip.
New tendon research says there's no single best rep range or exercise, training needs to be personalized.
Outside magazine says a few genuinely affordable climbing towns still exist, if anyone's weighing a lifestyle move.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Pregnancy Infections, Sleep Science, and New Parent Benefits
blocks.script:
A Swedish study is worth knowing if you have clients expecting a baby or a pregnant daughter to support. Researchers tracked 3.7 million people and looked at TORCH infections, a group of rare infections including toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes that can pass from a pregnant woman to a fetus. ScienceDaily reports that children with a congenital TORCH infection were about three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism, more than seven times more likely to have an intellectual disability, and up to thirty times more likely to have severe to profound intellectual disability. The word to hold onto is rare. These infections are uncommon, and standard prenatal screening already catches most of them. The useful conversation point is that consistent prenatal care matters, not that this is a new source of anxiety.

Separately, ScienceDaily covered a sleep study tracking more than 95,000 people. More time in REM sleep, the dreaming stage, was linked to lower risk of 83 conditions including dementia and heart failure, while more deep sleep tracked with lower risk of type 2 diabetes and depression. It is an adult study, not a paediatric one, but it backs up standard paediatric advice on protecting sleep architecture in kids: consistent bedtimes, dark rooms, no screens before bed. That is not just about next day tantrums, it may carry forward for decades.

On the family side, the Globe and Mail's advice column today answers a parent who suspects an ex is badmouthing them to their son. The columnist notes it is normal for teens dealing with parental separation to have emotional swings, and points toward documenting concerns calmly rather than confronting the child directly. For clients going through separation with kids in the house, that is a useful frame. Courts and mediators care about consistency, not who wins an argument with a teenager.

On the money side, two updates worth having ready. Employment Insurance parental benefits: standard pays 55 percent of earnings up to 729 dollars a week for up to 35 weeks, extended pays 33 percent up to 437 dollars a week for up to 61 weeks, and both parents can share extra weeks. The Canada Child Benefit rose again this July: up to 8,157 dollars a year for a child under six, 6,883 for a child six to seventeen, phasing out gradually above roughly 38,000 dollars in family net income. blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Discounted cash flow: the mechanics in five inputs / Pension income splitting and the pension credit / Causal chaining: making one idea lead to the next so the listener cannot stop
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 3: Discounted cash flow: the mechanics in five inputs.

The discounted cash flow model is the one every analyst claims to trust more than P/E or EV to EBITDA, because it's supposed to value the business itself, not the market's mood about it. But it only has five moving parts. If you don't know where each one comes from, you're not modeling, you're guessing with extra steps.

First input: free cash flow, the cash left after the business pays for the capital it needs to keep running. Operating cash flow minus capital expenditures, straight off the cash flow statement. On Thomson ONE, that sits in the estimates screen if you want consensus figures instead of building your own from the filings.

Second: the growth rate for those cash flows across your forecast window, usually five to ten years.

Third: the discount rate, your cost of capital, telling you what a dollar five years out is worth today. We build that properly tomorrow.

Fourth: terminal value, the lump sum standing in for everything after your forecast window, usually a perpetuity growth rate near long run GDP growth, 2 to 3 percent.

Fifth: shares outstanding, to move from total enterprise value to a per share figure.

Here's the arithmetic. Say a company generates 500 million dollars in free cash flow this year, growing 6 percent annually for five years. Discount those five years back at a 9 percent cost of capital. Take year five's cash flow, grow it 2.5 percent into perpetuity, and discount that lump sum back too. Add both pieces, subtract net debt, divide by shares outstanding. That's your intrinsic value per share.

The one mistake almost everyone makes: terminal value usually accounts for 60 to 75 percent of total value in the model, and people build it on a single growth assumption they never stress test. Move that rate from 2 to 3 percent and the valuation can swing 20 percent or more. Your five year forecast is precise. Your terminal value is a guess wearing a suit.

What this reveals: whether the current price assumes cash generation the business can plausibly deliver. What it cannot do: replace judgment about that assumption with false precision, no matter how many decimal places the spreadsheet shows.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 10: Pension income splitting and the pension credit.

Pension income splitting lets a couple move up to fifty percent of one spouse's eligible pension income onto the other spouse's tax return, purely on paper, to lower the household's total tax bill. It's a joint election made every year, form T1032, filed with the T1. No money actually moves.

For 2026, what counts as eligible depends on age. If the pension recipient is 65 or older, eligible income includes registered retirement income fund withdrawals, called a RIF, registered pension plan payments, and certain annuity payments. Under 65, only lifetime annuity payments from a registered pension plan qualify, a RIF withdrawal does not count yet. Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security are never eligible for this election. Those use a separate mechanism called CPP pension sharing, a different application entirely.

Now the credit. Anyone with eligible pension income can claim the pension income amount, a federal non-refundable credit on the first two thousand dollars of that income, worth roughly three hundred dollars in actual tax savings. That two thousand dollar figure hasn't moved in years and isn't indexed. Manitoba has its own version, a one thousand dollar provincial pension income amount, claimed the same way on the provincial return.

Here's the worked example. One spouse, age 68, withdraws forty thousand dollars from a RIF in 2026 and has no other income. The other spouse has ten thousand dollars of income. Splitting fifty percent moves twenty thousand dollars to the lower income spouse. That drops the RIF spouse's taxable income and gives the second spouse their own two thousand dollar pension credit, which they couldn't claim before since they had no pension income of their own. Together this can save several hundred dollars in tax, and for higher earners it can also pull net income under the Old Age Security clawback threshold from last lesson.

The mistake people make: assuming RIF income before age 65 qualifies for splitting. It doesn't. Before 65, only pension income from a registered pension plan is splittable, not a personal RIF.

Communication, lesson 10: Causal chaining: making one idea lead to the next so the listener cannot stop.

Randy Olson spent over a decade as a tenured marine biology professor before he quit to attend film school at the University of Southern California. He wanted to know why scientists could not get anyone to listen. He studied thousands of scripts and speeches and found that the highest-performing ones share a pattern built on three words: and, but, therefore. He calls it the ABT structure. Weak communication runs on "and": this happened, and this happened, and this happened. It is a list. Strong communication runs on: this is true, but this complicates it, therefore this follows. Each clause opens a question the next one answers, so the listener cannot leave the sentence unfinished in their head.

Here is the worked version. Say you are explaining a client's portfolio shift. Weak version: your allocation was 70 percent equities, and the market fell 12 percent in the third quarter of 2025, and we moved you into bonds. Three ands, no pull. Chained version: your allocation was 70 percent equities, but when the market fell 12 percent in the third quarter, that exposure meant your account absorbed most of the loss, therefore we shifted 15 percent into short-duration bonds to cut that exposure in half. Same facts. One version invites the next sentence. The other invites a nod and a glance at the clock.

The mistake is using "however" or "so" as furniture, a transition word placed where no real pivot exists. If the clause after "but" has no actual tension, and the clause after "therefore" is not a real consequence of it, you have not chained anything, you have just decorated a list.

Your task today: take one explanation you gave this week using and, and, and, and rewrite it in three sentences using and, but, therefore. Say it out loud once before you move on.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull last year's tax return for a client over 65 who has RIF income, check line for the pension income amount, and confirm whether form T1032 was actually filed to split income with their spouse.
Communication: Rewrite one recent explanation from a string of "and" sentences into the and, but, therefore structure, and say the new version out loud once.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Macklem's Tariff Warning Shadows Rate Path
blocks.script:
Tiff Macklem gave the line advisors should be repeating to clients this week. Speaking in Halifax on Monday, the Bank of Canada governor said that if the latest round of US tariffs stays in place, Canada's fourth quarter growth rate could be roughly halved, down to below one per cent. That is a sharp step down from the second quarter's three point three per cent annualized pace, the fastest since early 2023. Macklem said businesses had just started looking past the trade war toward opportunity, but the newest fifty per cent tariffs on nearly twenty eight billion dollars of Canadian goods risk pushing companies back into what he called the reassessment stage: delayed hiring, delayed investment. On rates, the Bank held at two point two five per cent this month, the seventh straight hold, and the next scheduled decision is October twenty eighth. That is on the watch list, and it lands with a full Monetary Policy Report, so expect a real reset of the growth and inflation forecasts, not just a rate call. Macklem also flagged the harder problem: oil near one hundred dollars a barrel is pushing gas prices up, and if that holds he expects inflation to edge higher even as growth slows.

Markets gave you some relief yesterday. The TSX closed up about six tenths of a per cent, just over thirty six thousand, led by Shopify and BlackBerry, both up more than seven per cent. In New York, the Nasdaq jumped two point three per cent to a fresh record close, the S&P gained one point five, riding a renewed AI trade after Meta's stock surged eleven per cent on its new Muse tool.

Oil is the one to watch for inflation-sensitive clients. West Texas crude fell over four per cent to under ninety two dollars after Saudi Arabia moved to restart its East-West pipeline and reports surfaced that Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington eases pressure. That is disinflationary if it holds, and it is worth mentioning at the next portfolio review.

The loonie is the weak spot. It touched a nearly seven week low against the US dollar, trading near seventy one cents, or one point four zero per US dollar, even with Macklem sounding firmer on inflation risk. Widening yield spreads with the US are doing the damage.

On policy, Ottawa tabled its Building Canada Strong Act this week, promising one year federal reviews for major projects, while Trump keeps floating tariff threats over Canada's widening alliances abroad. More headlines are coming before that October rate decision, not fewer.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Telesat, Capital Power, Anthropic Lead Business News
blocks.script:
Telesat is the story with the most riding on it right now. The Canadian satellite operator, builder of the Lightspeed low earth orbit broadband constellation, is squaring off with American creditors over its debt load, and the Globe and Mail reports the company could default on its loans if it can't reach an agreement. That matters because Telesat was the company Mark Carney's team put in front of foreign investors at his investment summit as a flagship Canadian tech bet. The tailwind is government backing and strategic broadband demand. The headwind is a capital structure built for a lower rate world colliding with skeptical American lenders. An evidence-based advisor tells you this is a single-name credit story with government exposure, not something to hold outside a small speculative sleeve.

Capital Power is the utility at the center of today's Report on Business feature, run by chief executive Avik Dey, and it is Canada's largest independent power producer. The Globe profile puts him at the centre of an electrical storm in Alberta, where the push for data centres to capitalize on its abundance of power is meeting resistance from worried ratepayers, including a virtual power supply deal tied to Meta's Sturgeon County data centre. The tailwind is years of AI driven electricity demand. The headwind is political blowback over rates and the regulatory roadblocks Dey himself says still need clearing. An advisor would say the AI power theme is real, but buy the utility sector broadly rather than betting on one Alberta generator.

Anthropic makes the Claude family of AI models and is backed by Amazon and Google. It just unveiled Claude Opus 5.5, which the Globe reports delivers performance close to its top tier Fable 5.1 model while costing 40 per cent less to run than its predecessor. The tailwind is cheaper inference widening enterprise adoption just as OpenAI and Alibaba push out competing models ahead of a China-US leaders' meeting. The headwind is a price war compressing margins across the entire sector. An evidence-based advisor says private AI labs are not investable directly for most clients, so get the exposure through a diversified fund, not a story.

LVMH and Kering are the two biggest names in global luxury, LVMH owning Louis Vuitton and Dior, Kering owning Gucci. Milan and Paris fashion weeks are underway, and Reuters reporting carried by the Globe shows shares in Gucci owner Kering have erased all the gains made when CEO Luca de Meo took the helm a year ago, while LVMH, the biggest luxury group, is down 37 per cent since the start of 2026. The tailwind is brands doubling down on their wealthiest customers with exclusive store experiences. The headwind is middle class shoppers pulling back and Middle East driven inflation squeezing budgets. An advisor tells you this is a sector recovery story with no clear timeline, size it as a small satellite position at most.

Saudi Aramco operates the East-West pipeline that lets Saudi crude reach Red Sea export terminals without transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The Globe reports sources say that pipeline is close to coming back online after a drone attack forced a shutdown that had been rerouting close to 4 per cent of global supply, right as Donald Trump backs a US diesel export ban with fuel prices at record highs. The tailwind is restored Saudi flows easing part of the squeeze. The headwind is that Russian and Iranian exports remain war disrupted, so diesel stays tight regardless. An advisor says energy is a volatile satellite holding for most portfolios, not a core position.

Empire owns Sobeys, Safeway and other grocery banners across Canada. It has reached a legally binding deal with the Competition Bureau to end its use of property controls, an agreement that will stop the grocer from enforcing land restrictions or exclusivity clauses that kept competitors out of its real estate. The tailwind is that this removes an antitrust overhang hanging over the stock. The headwind is that it signals more regulatory scrutiny is coming for the whole grocery sector. An advisor would tell you grocery names are steady dividend payers, but don't overweight one grocer while policy risk is this active.

Ontario Power Generation runs the Pickering nuclear station, a Crown utility supplying a large share of the province's electricity. Pickering has shut down for refurbishment, and the Globe reports Ontario expects gas fired plants, which carry higher marginal costs, to fill a larger share of the gap, raising fears of higher power prices. The tailwind is that refurbishment protects decades of future nuclear capacity. The headwind is near term reliance on costlier gas generation just as demand keeps climbing. An advisor says you can't buy this Crown utility directly, but the rate risk belongs in any Ontario household's financial plan.

The Securities and Exchange Commission is the top securities regulator in the United States. Globe commentary argues its push to gut shareholder proposals is censoring investors to shield companies from scrutiny, and warns it sets a dangerous precedent Canadian regulators could copy. The tailwind, if you're management, is less activist noise. The headwind, if you're an owner, is losing a tool shareholders use to flag governance risk before it becomes a financial problem. An advisor tells you to keep voting your proxies and using engaged fund managers, and not assume regulators will keep protecting those tools indefinitely.

Hiive, the Vancouver built marketplace for trading private company stock, has renamed itself Clarity as it plans an expansion. The Globe reports the company is on track to surpass 100 million US dollars in revenue facilitating trades of private tech giants that are staying off public markets longer. The tailwind is investor appetite for pre-IPO exposure to companies like OpenAI and SpaceX. The headwind is that private markets carry wide spreads and thin disclosure compared with listed stocks. An advisor says this is an interesting tool for accredited investors, but it's not a substitute for a diversified, liquid core portfolio.

High Art Capital is an Ontario backed real estate fund, and it just paid 22.3 million dollars for 43 unsold Toronto condo units, a bulk purchase well below market rate and one of the few such deals ever disclosed publicly. The tailwind is that a motivated seller taking this discount could help set a price floor for a soft condo market. The headwind is that the discount itself confirms how weak new construction demand really is in Toronto right now. An advisor would say bulk distressed deals like this are built for professional real estate funds, not something a retail client can access or should try to copy.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: CIRO's Big Fines, Ottawa's New Deduction, Manitoba's Grocery Tax Cut
blocks.script:
Start with enforcement, because the numbers are big enough to matter for your compliance file. CIRO, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, closed out its fiscal year with 7.6 million dollars in sanctions against individual advisors and another 8.6 million against firms. That came out of 39 decisions, with 10 permanent bars and 16 suspensions handed down by hearing panels. If you have junior staff who treat enforcement bulletins as background noise, this is the year to walk them through a couple of the case summaries. The regulator is also flagging a proficiency overhaul and a cyber-related lawsuit in the same wrap-up, so expect more scrutiny on both fronts heading into next year.

Separately, the Canadian Forum for Financial Markets is warning that Canada's capital markets fee structure is fragmented and expensive, and needs an overhaul to keep investment here rather than losing it to other jurisdictions. Worth knowing if clients ask why Canadian listings feel thin compared to the U.S.

On the legal side, an Alberta court has refused to put an end to the NaturEner wind farm dispute, a fight that traces back to a 2007 sale and is still generating litigation two decades later. Not urgent for your book, but a good reminder to clients that infrastructure and renewable deals carry long tails.

Now, client protection. Payments Canada research shows Gen Z Canadians are losing money to fraud at twice the national rate, a sharp generational split that should reshape how you talk to younger clients and their parents about payment security, not just their portfolios.

On the practice side, a Maximizer webinar found that clients want more from their advisor directly, not more from an AI layer between you and them. That lines up with what you're probably feeling already: automation buys you time, but the relationship is still the product.

And on savings, a new Scotiabank poll, worth flagging since Scotia's wealth arm is one to watch this year, found that even as Canadians tell surveys nobody is saving, the vast majority actually are. The real gap is turning that saved cash into invested wealth, which is an opening for exactly the kind of conversation you have every day.

Now to tax, because there's a genuine federal change worth knowing cold. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced on September 14th that the Canada Revenue Agency will prioritize responses to advance income tax ruling requests related to investments of $1 billion or more in Canada, effective immediately. The next day, the Department of Finance released draft legislative proposals to implement the newly announced Productivity Mega Deduction, which provides immediate expensing for a broad range of depreciable property acquired and available for use after September 14th. For your incorporated business owner clients, that's a capital expenditure timing question worth raising this quarter, before year-end planning conversations lock in.

Closer to home, Manitoba's spring budget is still working through the system. There are no proposed changes to the corporate tax rates or the $500,000 small business limit, though the budget introduces new affordability measures including changes to retail sales tax. Specifically, retail sales tax was removed from additional food and beverages sold by grocery stores and from prenatal vitamins, effective July 1st. On the credit side, the Renters Affordability Tax Credit rose to 625 dollars for 2026, moving to 675 dollars for 2027. Useful detail for incorporated professional clients who rent rather than own, and for anyone doing a Manitoba-specific plan this fall.

Shifting to bigger themes. The Globe is running a piece asking how long Canada can keep 65 as the normal retirement age, given that many developed countries are pushing theirs higher. Good conversation starter with clients in their late fifties who assume 65 is still the default finish line.

On housing, rents in the ten Canadian cities most exposed to U.S. tariffs have dropped about three per cent since last January, faster than in cities less exposed to the trade war, per the Globe. If you have clients relocating for work or downsizing, that's a real number to bring into the conversation, not just a headline.

On product trends, the latest S&P index scorecard shows professional money managers still lagging the S&P 500, again, reinforcing the case for low-cost indexing that a lot of your clients already believe in.

Quick market notes. The S&P 500 rose one point four nine per cent yesterday, but thirty stocks in the index still hit new lows, a reminder that headline gains can mask a lot of internal churn. Potash stocks dropped four per cent after Donald Trump pitched buying from Belarus at a lower price, though Belarus's president says supply is already spoken for. And a European lender is looking at Canadian critical minerals for the first time, part of a broader move by fund managers toward neutral on Canada as the TSX trades below U.S. multiples.

On the industry side, Richardson Wealth is rebranding to Nobelia Wealth effective November 30th, following its acquisition by iA Financial last year. If clients ask why statements look different this winter, that's the reason.

Two more things. Service Canada issues OAS and CPP payments this Friday, so expect the usual round of client calls about amounts and timing. And Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem is on the watch list this week after warning that if U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods stay in place, fourth quarter growth could get cut roughly in half, below one per cent, which complicates the rate path for the rest of the year.
talkingPoints: Ask incorporated clients if they have capital purchases planned, the new federal expensing deduction may change the timing.

Manitoba's grocery and prenatal vitamin sales tax relief has been in effect since July, worth confirming clients know.
Gen Z clients are getting defrauded at twice the national rate, raise payment security with younger family members.
Richardson Wealth becomes Nobelia Wealth on November 30th, flag it before clients notice the name change themselves.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Deficit Halves, Wyatt Runs, Dynacare Ruling Looms
blocks.script:
Manitoba's books look better than advertised, and that's the headline for anyone with money in this province. The audited public accounts show the deficit for the last fiscal year came in at 832 million dollars. That's nearly half the 1.67 billion dollar shortfall the province had forecast back in December, and it lines up with the 794 million dollar estimate in this year's budget. Finance Minister Adrien Sala called it moving in the right direction, and Premier Wab Kinew says the province is on track to balance the budget next year. For your clients watching Manitoba bonds or provincial spending, that's a real tightening, not just spin.

And it's landing well politically. A new Free Press, Abacus Data poll has Kinew and the NDP at their highest support level yet, buoyed by gains outside Winnipeg, while Obby Khan's Tories keep losing ground. If you're fielding questions about policy stability heading into next year's provincial budget, that poll matters. Political risk in Manitoba right now looks low.

Now, two settlements that are going to come up at dinner tables this week because they're eye-popping numbers. The Free Press and CBC both report Manitoba paid three First Nations men, Brian Anderson, Allan Woodhouse, and Clarence Woodhouse, four million dollars apiece for their wrongful conviction in the 1973 killing of restaurant worker Ting Fong Chan. That's on top of a separate seven million dollar payment the City of Winnipeg is contributing to the same global settlement. Separately, two men switched at birth in a rural Manitoba hospital back in 1955 were paid 250,000 dollars each in this fiscal year, according to the province's financial disclosures. These are the kinds of legacy liabilities that show up in public accounts and remind you the province is still settling very old files.

On labour, the Manitoba Labour Board heard closing submissions yesterday on whether Dynacare lab workers count as essential. This is the private lab company that does about 40 percent of diagnostic testing in the province. The province intervened right after roughly 350 workers walked out on strike this month, and the board ordered them back on the job within a day while it decides. The board says it will rule by October 1st. If Dynacare workers get designated essential, that curbs their strike leverage going forward, and it's already got the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals accusing the NDP government of overreach. Worth watching if any of your clients touch health care staffing or public sector labour contracts.

On the political front here in Winnipeg, the municipal election just got real. Twelve candidates have now completed the process to get on the mayoral ballot. Incumbent Scott Gillingham used nomination deadline day to promise a long term revitalization strategy for a stretch of Main Street from West Kildonan down to city hall. Challenger Kevin Klein raised concerns the same day about a change to how Transit Plus drivers are classified, calling it an anti-worker move. Meanwhile Transcona councillor Russ Wyatt filed to run again despite facing sexual assault charges, and that's drawn a public denunciation from fellow councillors and labour leaders who say his continued presence would be, in their words, a legal drama for the ward.

One more political story with some sting to it: a Progressive Conservative candidate, Serena Klos, is accusing the Manitoba Teachers' Society of pushing her out as an executive member and Sunrise School Division association president because she's running for the Tories. That's a governance story worth knowing if you sit on any board with union representation questions.

A few quick smaller items. The province announced new funding through Red River College Polytech for American Sign Language education and training aimed at Indigenous women. There's also a new Premier's Fitness Challenge for schools, with up to 10,000 dollars on offer for participating schools. And Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list today: its board members are out visiting First Nations communities this week to discuss damage from past hydro developments, a sign that reconciliation costs around Hydro infrastructure aren't going away.

Elsewhere, an Interlake First Nation is asking licensed moose hunters to voluntarily turn in their tags over a shrinking moose population. Steinbach blocked a local plebiscite on cannabis retail. Three people face kidnapping charges after a knifepoint incident in Flin Flon. And on the Winnipeg Jets, on the watch list too, the team dropped its home preseason finale two-one in overtime to Edmonton last night, with roster cuts expected as early as today ahead of the regular season opener against Boston on October 2nd. The Blue Bombers, also on the list, had backup quarterback Brown taking first team reps in practice as Collaros continues recovering from a head injury.
talkingPoints: Manitoba's deficit came in at 832 million, half what was forecast, and the province says it's on track to balance next year.
Three men wrongfully convicted in 1973 got four million each from the province, plus a separate seven million from the city.
Dynacare's essential services ruling lands by October 1st, and it could reshape strike rights for lab workers province wide.
Twelve names are now on the Winnipeg mayoral ballot, with Gillingham pitching a Main Street revitalization plan.
Manitoba Hydro board members are touring First Nations this week to talk past development damage, reconciliation costs are still live.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: Carney's Fall Fights and the Prairie Angle
blocks.script:
Mark Carney is picking three fights at once this fall, and each one touches your clients' portfolios in a different way, so it's worth walking through all three.

On Monday the government tabled Bill C-39, a two hundred and forty six page omnibus bill. The bill seeks to end what critics maintain is an unwieldy approvals process for major projects and establish a one-year timeline for federal reviews. Carney faced reporters Tuesday and didn't back down. He says his government received a clear mandate from voters in the last general election, and in subsequent byelections, to build Canada strong, and he's pressing ahead with changes to federal project approvals and the Labour Code despite criticism from some circles. His own words: "A decision delayed is a project denied," Carney said. "If you're going to say no, decide it within a year." On the labour side, Carney said the bill "absolutely reinforces the right to strike," but the Canadian Labour Congress disagrees, and unions say a new clause lets the minister end a strike deemed against the national interest. The Conservatives are drawing comparisons to Stephen Harper's 2012 omnibus bill, but the polling backdrop is different: Harper was in the mid-thirties then, Carney is averaging 46 percent now. Watch this bill through committee this fall, it touches ports, pipelines, and mines.

On pipelines specifically, Ottawa has offered Indigenous groups along the Trans Mountain route a combined 15 percent equity stake, according to the Globe and Mail, with each community also offered a 2.5 million dollar payment once it formally commits to invest. Finance Minister confirmed the government is also reviewing how it eventually sells its stake in Trans Mountain altogether. For prairie-adjacent clients with exposure to energy infrastructure, this is the mechanism Ottawa is using to buy social license for the next wave of projects, watch whether other corridors get the same treatment.

Closer to home, there's a study out of Saskatoon that matters for Manitoba. New EY analysis released by Protein Industries Canada found Canada could generate up to 5.4 billion dollars in additional GDP and support approximately 34,000 full-time-equivalent jobs by redirecting just 10 per cent of its raw crop exports to value-added processing here at home. That same shift could add 7.9 billion dollars in additional Canadian food manufacturing output and up to 1.1 billion dollars in government revenue. In 2024, Canada shipped 88 per cent of its food exports to the U.S., with the U.S. and China the biggest importers at 32 and 18 per cent respectively. Manitoba's canola crushing and protein processing plants sit right in the middle of this argument, it's the kind of federal priority that could shape provincial investment attraction for years.

On trade, India's High Commissioner told the Globe and Mail he expects Prime Minister Modi to visit Canada in December to sign a completed free trade deal, with the agreement itself wrapped up by November. He expects side deals on defence and aerospace to be signed during the same visit, and more detail on the Talent and Innovation Strategy launched in February. Carney confirmed the timeline Tuesday. This caps a genuine repair job between Ottawa and New Delhi after a very cold stretch, and it's Carney's clearest non-U.S. trade diversification win so far.

In British Columbia, Premier David Eby has called a snap election for October 24th, framing it as a response to Donald Trump's trade threats and calling it an existential moment for the province. It comes right after the BC Conservatives went through weeks of chaos, four dissident MLAs rejoining the party just as the writ dropped. Worth watching if you have BC-exposed clients, this race is being fought explicitly on who can stand up to Washington.

Back in Ottawa, several seniors were arrested on Parliament Hill during a climate protest, members of a self-described climate caravan charged with trespassing. It's a small story but it fits the season, Parliament is back, and every one of these fall bills is drawing a crowd outside the building as well as inside it.
talkingPoints: Bill C-39 is the big one this fall, it touches project approvals and the right to strike together.
Carney is betting his 46 percent polling number gives him room that Harper never had at similar bills.
Ottawa's 15 percent Trans Mountain equity offer to First Nations is the template for buying in on future corridors.
A new EY study says processing more crops at home could add over 5 billion dollars in GDP, that's a prairie story.
BC's October 24th election is being framed entirely around who can stand up to Trump.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Pregnancy Training Science, Wearables, and Rescue Tech
blocks.script:
New research out of a sport science conference in Toronto is upending old advice on exercise during pregnancy. Outside reports that Margie Davenport of the University of Alberta and Michelle Mottola of Western University shared data showing recreational weightlifting above 20 pounds is now linked to lower rates of gestational hypertension, diabetes, mood disorders, and excessive fetal growth, reversing decades of caution built on workplace lifting studies rather than gym training. One trial had just 15 participants testing high intensity interval training, short bursts near maximum heart rate, and found both mother and baby tolerated it fine. That is a small, early study, not a new guideline yet, but it lines up with a growing body of work saying moderate to heavy training during pregnancy may do less harm than stopping cold.

On the training side, Outside has a three minute drill this week aimed at calf and Achilles tightness, the kind of nagging stiffness that shows up after long runs or heavy squat days. It is built around slow isometric holds and controlled calf raises rather than static stretching, which tracks with what physical therapists have been saying for years: tendons respond to load, not just flexibility work.

On the gear front, Apple's new Watch Ultra 4 is out, and the headline claim is accuracy. Apple says a study of more than a thousand participants shows it beats other wrist wearables on heart rate sensing, now sampled every five seconds, feeding a new readiness score. Battery life moves up to 50 hours in standard use and 45 hours during an outdoor workout with full GPS. Independent reviewer DC Rainmaker, who tested it directly, says the optical sensor is the best Apple has built, though he is skeptical of the exact one beat per minute edge Apple claims over rivals, since the comparison methods differ. Good hardware, marketing claim worth a discount.

On the Canadian health system side, CBC reports a City of Calgary review found 911 dispatch mistakes delayed the search for eleven year old Parker Wells by roughly an hour this summer. He went missing from a care facility in July and was found two weeks later in an underground pipe system. It is a hard story, and it is prompting a real look at dispatch procedures.

CBC also profiled Atlantic Canada's LifeFlight air ambulance service, which has flown critically ill and injured patients for three decades, easing pressure on hospitals across the region when ground transport would take too long.

Three quick items worth knowing. In Colorado, rescuers used spotlight drones and a rope system to reach a UTV driver, that is utility task vehicle, who tumbled 250 feet down a slope, a reminder of how much drone tech has changed backcountry rescue. In New Jersey, Ocean City hired falcons to chase off seagulls harassing beachgoers, and so far it is working. And Outside notes climate change is scrambling fall foliage timing in national parks, making the old leaf peeping calendars less reliable.
talkingPoints: Pregnancy training guidelines may loosen, but the underlying studies are still small.
Achilles and calf pain responds better to loaded holds than passive stretching.
New Apple Watch claims best in class heart rate accuracy, independent testers are half convinced.
A Calgary dispatch review found real delays in the Parker Wells search.
Atlantic Canada's air ambulance service quietly takes pressure off rural hospitals.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Coffee, Sleep Science, and a Father-Son Road Trip
blocks.script:
You know that feeling of falling asleep fine after an evening coffee and still waking up flat. A new systematic review out of Wroclaw Medical University, published this year in the journal Nutrients, explains why. Researchers led by Professor Donata Kurpas pooled thirty two studies and found that caffeine keeps suppressing the slow brain waves tied to deep, restorative sleep, even when you fall asleep on schedule and stay in bed the full eight hours.

Caffeine reduces the depth of sleep even if total sleep time appears normal, so patients might sleep the entire night but still wake up feeling exhausted. The review found the disruption is worst in recovery sleep after sleep deprivation, with a weaker than expected rebound in slow-wave activity, which is exactly the kind of night new parents are chasing after a wake up with an infant. And individual responses vary depending on genetics and metabolism, so what wrecks one partner's sleep barely touches the other.

It is not only adults. A separate paediatric study of ten to sixteen year olds found caffeine consumers had later habitual bedtimes and less time in bed compared to non-consumers, alongside a twenty percent average reduction in slow-wave activity at the start of the night, even though the effect disappeared by morning and tiredness was unaffected. If there is a teenager in the house leaning on energy drinks before exams, that is a fair thing to raise over dinner tonight.

On the lighter side, the Globe and Mail profiles a Calgary father and son, John and Spencer van Roessel, who did not get picked for Amazing Race Canada and built their own instead. Seventeen days, nineteen stops, close to sixteen thousand kilometres coast to coast, including a Father's Day bungee jump in Chelsea, Quebec, Spencer's most memorable part of the trip. The expensive family vacation is not the only model. A tight budget and a shared goal produced what sounds like the better memory.

Also today: Canadian designer Edeline Lee turned her old high school gym into her atelier to launch her London collection, carrying over the discipline of her ballet training. And the Globe explains ghost posting, where users resurface archived posts to sidestep Instagram's algorithm, useful to know if you are trying to figure out what your teenager is actually doing on their phone. Your horoscope for today is out too, for what that is worth.
talkingPoints: Caffeine can quietly blunt deep sleep even when you feel rested, ask clients with young kids how they are actually sleeping, not just how long.
Teen caffeine use tracks with later bedtimes and shallower sleep, a plain fact for the dinner table.
A structured, budget-first family trip can outperform an expensive one for memory value.
Ghost posting is now a thing your teenager's feed runs on, worth a passing question at home.
If year end planning is coming up, it is a good moment to check RESP contribution room alongside other family goals.

blocks.label: Sports
blocks.title: Jets Fall in OT, Bombers Prep, Kawhi Re-Ups
blocks.script:
Start with the Jets, because the biggest hockey story in this city right now isn't a score, it's a goalie. Before we get there, last night's game: Winnipeg lost 2 to 1 in overtime to Edmonton at Canada Life Centre, the two teams' second preseason meeting in four days.

Alex Iafallo scored the lone goal for the Jets, and in overtime, Edmonton's Zach Hyman spotted Viljami Marjala on a two-on-one, and Marjala beat goaltender Domenic DiVincentiis at 1:26. Winnipeg wraps up its preseason Friday in Denver against the Colorado Avalanche. The Free Press has been tracking defenceman St. Ivany, who's trying to lock down a regular job on the back end this camp, a real storyline heading into the season. But the one dominating hockey talk across the league is Connor Hellebuyck. The Athletic reports the Jets goalie is one of two marquee players, along with Detroit's Dylan Larkin, who have asked their teams for a trade before puck drop next week. That is not a small story for a franchise built around its goaltending.

On the Blue Bombers side, Zach Collaros is still working back from a head injury, and backup Brown has been taking the bulk of the practice reps this week, per the Free Press. Hansen is also working his way back into the lineup on defence. The Bombers host the Toronto Argonauts at home this Friday night, a real game with playoff positioning on the line, not an exhibition.

Around the NHL, the coaching carousel kept spinning. The Associated Press reports Mike Babcock is back behind an NHL bench, part of a wave that saw the Oilers and four other clubs change coaches this off-season. Separately, the Globe and Mail reports the NHL's board of governors discussed possible expansion into Houston or Austin, Texas, but made no decision, and commissioner Gary Bettman gave no hint on when he might retire either. And for the world juniors crowd: the Globe reports Canada opens the 2027 tournament against Switzerland on Boxing Day, with games split between Edmonton and Red Deer.

Over in the NFL, the Rams handled the Giants 28-6 Monday night, and it was vintage everything: Matthew Stafford threw for 327 yards and four touchdowns, Davante Adams caught for 195 yards and two scores, and Aaron Donald played his first game in nearly three years. The bad news landed in New York. Quarterback Jaxson Dart left early with a knee injury that coach Brian Daboll, sorry, that Giants coach Harbaugh says is still being evaluated, with some reports suggesting it could be a sprained MCL. Jameis Winston is starting in his place for now.

In the NBA, Kawhi Leonard has signed a two-year, 115-million-dollar US extension with the Raptors, according to CBC and multiple outlets, a deal that reportedly includes a player option for 2028-29. That's the kind of number that gets asked about at every Toronto-adjacent dinner table this fall. In Houston, the Rockets are talking playoffs again now that Fred VanVleet is back healthy, with coach Ime Udoka wanting to see what a full roster can do.

A few more worth knowing if the conversation moves past the big four. The Chicago Sky snapped a five-game skid by beating the Toronto Tempo, per the Globe and Mail. The PWHL hired hockey attorney Alison Izzi as general manager of the Vancouver Goldeneyes. And in Montreal, the road cycling world championships are underway: Quebec's Vallieres Mill has a shot to become the first Canadian to defend a world title on home roads, while Canadian rider Derek Gee-West has withdrawn from Sunday's race after an injury.

Tonight itself is quiet on the local front. No Jets, no Bombers. The next dates that matter are Friday: Winnipeg closes its preseason in Denver against Colorado, and the Bombers host Toronto at home in a game that actually counts.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Balance sheet: working capital, and the three ratios that reveal stress / OAS: eligibility, the clawback threshold, and deferral math / Explaining risk: expected outcomes, ranges, and the language of probability
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 3: Balance sheet: working capital, and the three ratios that reveal stress.

Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It tells you whether a company can fund its own operations without borrowing more or selling something it needs. When it shrinks fast, that is usually the first place stress shows up, before it ever hits the income statement.

Three ratios do the real work here. First, the current ratio: current assets divided by current liabilities. Second, the quick ratio: same thing, but you strip out inventory, because inventory is the slowest asset to turn into cash. Third, the cash conversion cycle: days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding, minus days payable outstanding. That third one tells you how long cash is tied up before it comes back to the company.

Take a mid-cap industrial distributor. Current assets: 1.4 billion dollars. Current liabilities: 900 million. Current ratio is 1.56. Looks fine. Now strip inventory, which is 600 million of those current assets. Quick ratio drops to 0.89. That is below 1, meaning without selling inventory, the company cannot cover what it owes in the next twelve months. Then check the cash conversion cycle: 58 days inventory, 45 days receivables, 30 days payables. That is 73 days of cash tied up before it returns. If that number was 55 days two years ago, that is the story. In Thomson ONE, you get all three inputs off the balance sheet tab under Financials, and the DSO, DIO, DPO figures usually sit in the ratios or financial analysis section.

The mistake people make is reading the current ratio alone and calling it healthy. A current ratio above 1 hides a lot if inventory is bloated or slow moving. You need the quick ratio to see past that, and you need the cycle to see the trend, not just the snapshot.

Your task today: pull the last two fiscal years of balance sheet data for one company you know well, in Thomson ONE, and calculate all three ratios for both years. Fifteen minutes, no more. You are looking for direction, not a single number.

This tells you liquidity risk. It does not tell you profitability, and it does not tell you why cash is tied up. That comes next, with the cash flow statement.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 9: OAS: eligibility, the clawback threshold, and deferral math.

The single biggest OAS surprise for incorporated business owners is this: the clawback is based on taxable income, not cash income, and dividends get grossed up before that test applies. A business owner paying themselves eligible dividends can look modest on a bank statement and still get hammered on line 23600 of the tax return.

Here is how Old Age Security actually works. You qualify at 65 if you have lived in Canada at least 10 years after age 18. Full pension needs 40 years of residency after 18. Fewer years gives you a partial pension, one fortieth of the full amount per year of residency. For 2026, the maximum OAS payment at 65 is roughly 735 dollars a month, about 8,820 dollars a year, and it is indexed quarterly to inflation.

Now the clawback, officially the OAS Recovery Tax. For 2026, the threshold is approximately 95,800 dollars of net income. Above that line, you repay 15 cents of OAS for every dollar of income over the threshold, up to a full clawback around 155,000 dollars for someone 65 to 74.

Worked example. Client has net income of 130,000 dollars in 2026. That is 34,200 dollars over the 95,800 threshold. Multiply by 15 percent: 5,130 dollars gets clawed back over the following payment year. Against 8,820 dollars of annual OAS, that is 58 percent gone.

Deferral math is clean. Delay past 65 and OAS grows 0.6 percent per month, up to 60 months at age 70, for a maximum 36 percent increase. That turns 735 dollars into just over 1,000 dollars a month for life, and if income is high at 65 and drops later, deferral also sidesteps years of clawback.

The mistake: assuming OAS clawback tracks cash flow. It does not. Eligible dividends are grossed up by 38 percent before they hit net income, so a business owner drawing dividends can trigger clawback at a much lower real cash number than a T4 employee would.

Communication, lesson 9: Explaining risk: expected outcomes, ranges, and the language of probability.

In 1951, a CIA analyst named Sherman Kent wrote that a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia was a "serious possibility." Policymakers read that phrase and argued for weeks about what it meant. So Kent later surveyed his own colleagues and asked them to attach a number to "serious possibility." The answers ranged from 20 percent to 80 percent. Same words, wildly different meanings. That is the entire problem with explaining risk in language instead of numbers.

When you explain risk to a client, give three things every time: the expected outcome, the range around it, and a stated probability. Not adjectives. Numbers.

Here is a worked example. Say a client asks whether their portfolio will grow. Per S&P Dow Jones Indices, the S&P 500 has averaged roughly 10 percent a year since 1950. That is your expected outcome. But in any single year, returns have ranged from a loss of 37 percent in 2008 to a gain of 32 percent in 2013. That is your range. And historically, about one year in four has ended negative. That is your probability. So the honest sentence is: expect around 8 to 10 percent a year on average, but in any given year it could swing from a 20 percent loss to a 30 percent gain, and there is roughly a one in four chance it is a down year.

The mistake people make is collapsing all three into one confident number. "This will grow 8 percent." That is false precision. It sounds authoritative in the meeting and then it breaks trust the first year reality misses it, which undoes everything you built in the bad-news lesson.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull two fiscal years of balance sheet data for one company in Thomson ONE and calculate the current ratio, quick ratio, and cash conversion cycle for both years, noting the direction of change.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client's line 23600 from their most recent notice of assessment, compare it to the 95,800 dollar 2026 threshold, and note whether dividend gross-up is inflating that number relative to their actual cash income.
Communication: Take one outcome you regularly discuss with clients or board members, and write it as three sentences: expected value, range, and probability, each with a real number attached.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Markets Rally on AI Optimism, Oil Eases
blocks.script:
Good morning. Global markets started the week higher, lifted by a rally in technology stocks and a pullback in oil prices, as investors looked ahead to this week's summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

According to The Globe and Mail's Before the Bell newsletter, the pan-European STOXX 600 rose about one percent, with Britain's FTSE, Germany's DAX and France's CAC all posting gains. Hong Kong's Hang Seng also climbed, while Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

On Bay Street the mood was more mixed. The TSX slipped about 0.2 percent, while on Wall Street the S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged higher and the Dow dipped slightly, according to a market snapshot from The Peak. The Canadian dollar traded near 71.5 US cents.

Oil prices retreated from highs seen last week above 109 US dollars a barrel, with Brent and West Texas Intermediate both falling more than 2 percent on hopes of diplomatic progress on the Iran conflict, including a possible Trump meeting with Iran's president on the sidelines of this week's UN General Assembly, Bloomberg reported.

Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter also flagged growing unease about how much of the market's gains now rest on artificial intelligence. It noted AI-related spending accounts for roughly half of recent US GDP growth, and that nearly 33 trillion dollars has been added to S&P 500 valuations since late 2022, mostly tied to AI-linked companies. Fund managers told Bloomberg that diversifying away from that exposure has become difficult given how deeply AI is now woven through markets.

Feeding that boom, SoftBank is reportedly seeking to raise more than 11 billion dollars in what would be one of the largest junk bond deals ever, to help fund its investments in OpenAI.

Bloomberg also detailed a market meltdown in Turkey, where regulators cracked down on asset managers accused of artificially inflating illiquid stocks. Executives, including the chairman of asset manager Tera, have been arrested, and a finance company chairman's fortune, once valued near 14 billion dollars, is reportedly evaporating as authorities liquidate seized funds at steep discounts.

In corporate news, chipmaker AMD joined the trillion-dollar club, following Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron, on continued AI-driven demand, the Globe and Mail reported.

Paramount Skydance and California officials made progress in settlement talks over its 110 billion dollar acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, with terms reportedly including a commitment to release 30 films a year in theatres, the BBC reported.

And in Canadian wealth management, Richardson Wealth announced it will rebrand as Nobelia Wealth this November, following its acquisition by iA Financial last year.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem was scheduled to speak in Halifax today, with markets also watching Canada's July construction investment data.
talkingPoints: Global stocks rose on AI-led optimism and cooling oil prices ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
Oil pulled back on hopes of Iran diplomacy, though analysts warn the broader trend remains upward.
Bloomberg warns AI now underpins roughly half of US GDP growth and trillions in stock market gains, raising concentration risk.
SoftBank plans an over 11 billion dollar junk bond sale to fund further OpenAI investment.
Turkish regulators are unwinding funds accused of inflating illiquid stocks, wiping out fortunes.
AMD becomes the fourth US chipmaker to reach a trillion-dollar valuation.
Paramount and California near a settlement clearing its Warner Bros Discovery merger.
Richardson Wealth will become Nobelia Wealth in November under owner iA Financial.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: BlackBerry, Irving Oil, PSP Lead Canadian Business News
blocks.script:
BlackBerry is the story getting the most airtime in Canadian business circles right now. The Waterloo firm has rebuilt itself around embedded software for cars through its QNX platform, and the Globe and Mail reports it just secured a deal worth more than $100 million for a new automotive software product called Alloy Kore, landing before the product's official release later this year. The tailwind is obvious: a nine figure contract ahead of launch validates years of pivoting away from handsets and toward the car. The headwind is concentration risk, this is one customer, one product line, and the auto software space has deep pocketed rivals circling the same real estate inside every vehicle's dashboard. An evidence-based advisor would tell you a single contract headline is not a valuation, and that chasing the stock on the news release is speculation dressed up as analysis.

Irving Oil is next. The privately held Saint John refiner, one of the largest fuel suppliers in Atlantic Canada, has named Austrian energy executive Alfred Stern as its next chief executive, taking over November first from Jeff Matthews, who is retiring, the Globe reports, after a strategic review. The tailwind is a fresh, internationally seasoned hand brought in specifically after that review, suggesting the family ownership wants growth beyond the East Coast refinery footprint. The headwind is the review itself: when a private company brings in outside leadership after months of soul-searching, it usually means change is coming, and change at a company this size ripples through Atlantic Canada's fuel supply and jobs. An evidence-based advisor would simply note Irving Oil is private, so there is no ticker to buy, only indirect energy sector exposure through diversified funds.

Third is a story about airports, but really about who runs them. Montreal-based PSP Investments, the pension manager for federal public servants, already owns airports abroad through its AviAlliance subsidiary, and Globe commentary this week names it as the natural anchor for a global champion in a critical infrastructure sector once Ottawa sells concessions at Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal. The tailwind is scale and existing expertise, PSP already runs terminals overseas. The headwind is competition, other Canadian pension giants and foreign operators want the same concessions, and the politics of selling off national infrastructure are touchy. An evidence-based advisor would point out you likely already own a slice of this story through your own pension exposure, so there is nothing new to chase here.

StubHub is fourth. The ticket resale platform got hit with a $20,000 fine from Ontario, the Globe reports, under the province's new law capping resale prices, though the provincial website does not specify what events the penalties were linked to. The tailwind, if there is one, is that compliance signals the secondary ticket market is being taken seriously by regulators rather than ignored. The headwind is that this fine could be the first of many across provinces now watching resale pricing closely, and repeated penalties chip away at a platform's margins and reputation. An evidence-based advisor would say a $20,000 fine is immaterial to a company of StubHub's size, and headline regulatory risk should not drive a portfolio decision either way.

Fifth, a private rail bet on the Rockies. Liricon Capital and Plenary Americas have filed a passenger-rail proposal with the Alberta government for a Calgary-to-Banff line, the Globe reports, with the consortium saying it could be running by 2030. The tailwind is obvious tourist demand and a government that has been receptive to nation-building infrastructure pitches. The headwind is that Alberta has seen ambitious rail plans stall before, and financing, environmental review, and municipal buy-in all still need to fall into place. An evidence-based advisor would note this is a private consortium deal, not something retail investors can buy into directly, so treat it as a story to watch rather than a trade.

Sixth is Vero, an artificial intelligence tool built to lower legal costs for small business owners. The Globe reports critics say the technology is still young and isn't close to being able to replicate much of the work that lawyers do. The tailwind is real demand from small businesses priced out of legal advice. The headwind is liability, if the tool gets something wrong on a contract or a dispute, who is on the hook, and regulators overseeing legal practice are watching closely. An evidence-based advisor would call this an interesting signal of where professional services are heading, not an investable idea today, since it is a private venture with no public shares.

Last, the cannabis sector, led by names like High Tide, Canopy Growth and Aurora Cannabis. The Globe reports the industry is warning Ottawa that Canada could lose its lead in global cannabis exports without federal backing, with the sector forecasting two billion dollars in foreign sales by 2027. The tailwind is Canada's early regulatory head start and moves like High Tide's expansion into the German medical market. The headwind is the total absence of a federal export strategy, leaving producers to build international beachheads alone while global competitors catch up fast. An evidence-based advisor would remind a client these remain small, volatile stocks, sized as a speculative sliver of a portfolio, never a core holding.

None of tonight's watch list names, the Bank of Canada rate decision, Dimensional Fund Advisors, Scotia Wealth Management, Manitoba Hydro, United Way Winnipeg, the Jets or the Bombers, turned up in the business and markets coverage driving this block over the past 48 hours.

Irving Oil is bringing in an Austrian energy executive as CEO after a strategic review.
Ottawa's airport privatization plan could hand a Canadian pension fund a global infrastructure business.
StubHub just got fined by Ontario under the province's new ticket resale price cap.
Cannabis companies say Canada could lose its export lead without federal support.
